# Executive Summary

# Data Preparation

## Overview of the Dataset

The first step of the data exploration process is to load the insurance claims of our Belgian Motor Third Party Liability (MTPL) dataset.
We will start ensuring the uniqueness of keys. Straight after that, we will split the data between training and testing sets to make sure we keep a proper holdout for model evaluation.
Then, we'll have a look at our target variables and the distribution of the exposure.
Finally, we will have a quick look at the predictor variables we have before diving in the data transformation, exploration, and feature engineering.

<br>

### Uniqueness of Keys

Each row in the dataset represents a unique insurance policy (`ID`). We can verify the uniqueness of rows by checking if the number of unique `ID`s matches the total number of rows.
```{r uniqueness_of_rows, comment=NA}
setwd(paste0(
    "C:/Users/MathieuDemarets/Documents/UCL Certificat/",
    "CodeRepositories/LACTU2150/project"
))
load("../data/mtpl_be.rda")
data <- mtpl_be

n_unique_ids <- length(unique(mtpl_be$ID))
n_rows <- nrow(mtpl_be)
cat(sprintf(
    "Number of unique IDs: %d\nNumber of rows: %d\nAre they equal? %s", 
    n_unique_ids, n_rows, 
    ifelse(n_unique_ids == n_rows, "Yes", "No")
))

index_training <- createDataPartition(mtpl_be$NCLAIMS, times = 1, p = 0.8, list = FALSE) # Note that we make a single partition, cv will be done with the training set during modelling
data <- mtpl_be[index_training, ]
holdout <- mtpl_be[-index_training, ]
cat(sprintf(
    "Training set rows (data): %d\nTesting set rows (holdout): %d\n",
    nrow(data), nrow(holdout)
))
```

<br>

### Target Variables

For each policy, we have an exposure (`EXP`), which represents the fraction of the year that the policy was in force. The contract last a single year at most. Over that exposure time, we have the two target variables: 

- **Frequency (`NCLAIMS`)**: The number of claims filed during the policy period.
- **Severity (`AVG`)**: The average cost per claim during the policy period.

The total claim cost is derived from the frequency and severity:

- **Total Claim Cost (`NCLAIMS * AVG = AMOUNT`)**: The total cost of claims during the policy period.[^amount]

[^amount]: For policies with no claims, `AMOUNT` is zero; `AVG` is undefined.

```{r Exposure}
qtable <- function(data, x, n_quant) {
    data_not_na <- data[!is.na(data[[x]]), ]
    if (sum(is.na(data[[x]])) > 0) warning(sprintf("Removing %d NA values from column %s", sum(is.na(data[[x]])), x))
    # Get the n_quantiles of the column x
    qx <- quantile(data_not_na[[x]], probs = seq(0, 1, by = 1 / n_quant))
    quantiles <- data.frame(Quantile = names(qx), Value = as.numeric(qx))
    quantiles$Value <- format(quantiles$Value, big.mark = ",", format = "f", digits = 2, scientific = FALSE)
    rownames(quantiles) <- quantiles$Quantile
    quantiles$Quantile <- NULL    
    quantiles %>% t() %>% as.data.frame() %>% kable(
    caption = sprintf("Quantiles of %s", x),
    booktabs = FALSE
    ) %>% kableExtra::kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, position = "left")
}
```


```{r claims_distribution}
qtable(data, "NCLAIMS", 10)

p1 <- ggplot(data, aes(x = NCLAIMS)) +
    geom_bar() +
    labs(
        title = "NCLAIMS Distribution",
        x = "Number of Claims",
        y = sprintf("Count (All: %d)", nrow(data))
    ) +
    theme_minimal()

qtable(data, "AVG", 10)

filtered_AVG <- data %>% filter(!is.na(AVG))

p2 <- ggplot(filtered_AVG, aes(x = log(AVG))) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
    labs(
        title = "AVG Distribution",
        x = "Log of Average Claim Cost",
        y = sprintf("Count (All: %d)", nrow(filtered_AVG))
    ) +
    theme_minimal()

qtable(data, "AMOUNT", 10)

filtered_AMOUNT <- data %>% filter(!is.na(AMOUNT))
p3 <- ggplot(filtered_AMOUNT, aes(x = AMOUNT)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
    labs(
        title = "AMOUNT Distribution",
        x = "Total Claim Amount",
        y = sprintf("Count (All: %d)", nrow(filtered_AMOUNT))
    ) +
    theme_minimal()


(p1 | p3 )/ p2
```

For both the frequency and severity of claims, we observe a large distribution mass around zero. This is quite typical in insurance data, where many policies have no claims or very low average claim costs. We also note that `r sum(is.na(data$AVG))` policies have missing average claim costs.
This is simply because no claims were reported for these policies (`r sum(data$NCLAIMS == 0)` policies with no claims). The claim amount is by nature zero in this case, and the average ($\frac{AMOUNT}{NCLAIMS}$) is undefined and not informative. When we will tackle the modeling of claim severity, we will therefore focus only on policies with at least one claim.
To handle unbalanced data in the frequency modelling, various techniques are available such as:

- Synthetic oversampling techniques (e.g., SMOTE) create synthetic samples for the minority class to balance the dataset.
- Hurdle models can be employed to separately model the zero and non-zero counts, effectively handling the excess zeros in the data and focusing on the non-zero records in the second part of the model.

These are outside the scope of this analysis, it is nevertheless important to note that this unbalance will limit the frequency modelling performance and that these techniques could be explored in the future.

We can also note that the distribution of average claim is more interesting to look at. Indeed, we exclude policies with no claims, as their average claim is undefined. Then, we can take the logarithm of the average claim to better visualize the scale of cost instead of the absolute values.
The quantiles indeed show us a very skewed distribution, with most average claims being relatively low but a few policies having very high average claims. We can see two peaks in the log-transformed average claim distribution which indicates the presence of different kind of claims:

- First peak corresponds to small dents and repairs: the log around 5 represents claims of approximately `r sprintf("%.0f euros", exp(5))`
- Second peak corresponds to more significant repairs: the log around 7.5 represents claims of approximately `r sprintf("%.0f euros", exp(7.5))`
- Right tail corresponds to way bigger damages: the log around 10 represents claims of approximately `r sprintf("%.0f euros", exp(10))`

Even if they are not so frequent, the larger claims in the right tail can have a significant impact on the company profitability. A future report could use `Extreme Value Theory` to better model and understand these rare but impactful claims.

```{r exposure_distribution}
qtable(data, "EXP", 10)
```

Regarding the exposure, we see that a large majority of the policies have an exposure close to 1, indicating that most policies are active for nearly the entire year.
About `r 1-round(sum(data$EXP == 1) / nrow(data), 2)` of the policies have an exposure less than 1. This does not suggest that an analysis per exposure level is necessary.

Exposure should still be considered to correctly estimate the claim frequency as counting full exposure would underestimate the risk.
The correct way to compute the mean claim frequency is $$\frac{\sum{NCLAIMS}}{\sum{EXP}}, \text{ where } EXP \in [0, 1]$$ which will therefore be higher than the simple mean $$\frac{\sum{NCLAIMS}}{nrow(data) = \sum{1}}$$
```{r mean_frequency}
mean_claim_frequency <- sum(data$NCLAIMS) / sum(data$EXP)
se_mean <- sqrt(mean_claim_frequency / sum(data$EXP))
ic_99 <- mean_claim_frequency + c(-1, 1) * 2.576 * se_mean
wrong_mean <- mean(data$NCLAIMS)
cat(sprintf(
    "Correct mean claim frequency: %.3f%% (99%% CI: [%.3f%%, %.3f%%])\nNaive mean: %.3f%%",
    mean_claim_frequency * 100,
    ic_99[1] * 100,
    ic_99[2] * 100,
    wrong_mean * 100
))
```

This confirms that the naive mean of `NCLAIMS` falls short of the 99% confidence interval for the correct mean claim frequency. It is therefore crucial to account for the exposure through the offset[^offset] in the frequency modelling.

[^offset]: In frequency modelling, the exposure is typically included as an offset in the model to adjust for the varying lengths of policy coverage. This ensures that the estimated claim frequency accurately reflects the risk per unit of exposure rather than per policy.
